readingCallout.label: How to read this section
readingCallout.text: Layer 1 (suppliers) and Layer 3 (PlayBlue's actual layer) are not comparable on revenue — different margin structures, different jobs. The only chart below that is a fair apples-to-apples comparison is the Layer 2/3 retail-revenue chart in 5a. Everything else is shown as context, labelled as such.

retailCallout.label: What this chart actually says
retailCallout.text: PlayBlue's five-year ambition is 21% larger than Decathlon India's current business — built over sixteen years, capturing full margin where PlayBlue would capture retail margin only. Sports Station, the actual Layer 3 comparator, sits at ~4% of Decathlon after years of operating — the honest ceiling this model has demonstrated in India to date. The ₹100 Cr phase-one target is 58% of that ceiling, in year one.

layers.title: Layer 1 · Nike, Adidas, Puma, Asics, Yonex — suppliers
layers.desc: Sell wholesale to retailers including, potentially, PlayBlue. Compete only through their own flagship stores.

body.label: Position
body.text: Puma leads India at ₹3,274.8 Cr (CY23, up 10%) with 570+ stores, having overtaken Adidas in 2021 by localising hard — cricket sponsorships, Bollywood ambassadors, mass-market pricing. Only about a quarter of Puma's India revenue is sports performance; the rest is lifestyle and athleisure. Adidas continues to push its Indian national cricket team association; we found no verifiable current revenue figure for Adidas India and are not publishing one. Nike, the world's largest sportswear brand, has scaled back store count in India while retaining brand equity; likewise, no verifiable current revenue figure for Nike India.

body.label: Relationship to PlayBlue
body.text: Suppliers, and only channel-competitors where they run their own D2C stores — a narrow overlap, not a scale contest. Their India revenue is context for assortment planning (who to prioritise, what commercial terms are realistic) not a target to outgrow. Note what Puma's lead does say: in India, localisation and price accessibility beat pure global brand equity — worth carrying into how PlayBlue prices its own curation.

layers.title: Layer 2 · Decathlon — vertically integrated, legally single-brand
layers.desc: ₹4,133 Cr FY25 · ~130 stores · the price anchor and the format benchmark

body.label: Position
body.text: India's largest sports retail player. Big-box format, ~20 in-house brands it owns outright, aggressive pricing — a functional dry-fit t-shirt at ₹399. Financially it has swung between profit and loss across three years: FY23 net loss ₹18.6 Cr, FY24 net profit ₹197.2 Cr, FY25 net loss ₹65.0 Cr — one profitable year in three, on roughly 2–3% annual revenue growth.

body.label: Trajectory
body.text: €100M committed over five years. Expanding from ~110–132 to 190 stores across 90+ cities, targeting ~₹8,000 Cr by 2030. ~68% locally sourced in 2024, targeting 85% by 2026. Distributes through Ajio as well as own channels — and has reportedly petitioned the Indian government for multi-brand status so it can stock rival products such as Adidas and Garmin, confirming it currently cannot.

body.label: Why the model matters more than the number
body.text: Decathlon owns its brands, so it captures manufacturer margin plus retail margin, and its FDI classification as single-brand is a direct consequence of that structure. It sets the price anchor and format expectation PlayBlue must argue against, but it is not a like-for-like business-model comparator — it is the model PlayBlue is _not_ running.

layers.title: Layer 2 · Technosport and BlissClub — the vertically integrated challengers
layers.desc: Technosport ₹300–436 Cr (figures contested, see flag) · BlissClub ₹131.5 Cr FY25 (RoC filing) · both absent from PlayBlue's stated competitive framing

body.label: Technosport
body.text: Founded 2015 in Bengaluru. Revenue is reported as ₹436 Cr FY25 by one source and ₹300 Cr FY24 by another — both trace back to the same flagged aggregator (CEO Vine), so neither figure should be treated as confirmed until the MCA filing is pulled. Targets ₹600 Cr FY26. Reported to have raised ₹175 Cr from A91 Partners, though also reported elsewhere as $25M — verify via MCA/Tracxn before citing either figure. Controls its own manufacturing and fabric technology — moisture-wicking, anti-microbial, UV protection — selling performance wear at entry-level prices, effectively Decathlon's playbook run by a startup. 300 new stores announced on ₹200 Cr, directly contesting the same scarce retail space PlayBlue needs.

body.label: BlissClub
body.text: Founded 2020, women-first. Started with a single product — leggings designed for Indian women. Per RoC filing via Entrackr, audited figures show ₹131.5 Cr revenue FY25 (+51% YoY) and a ₹20 Cr net loss, down from a ₹44 Cr FY24 loss — replacing the company's previously stated ARR figure. Raised over $21M from Elevation Capital and Eight Roads, raising a further $25M.

body.label: Why they belong in this analysis
body.text: Structurally the same layer as Decathlon — own product, own manufacturing, own retail — not Layer 3 peers of PlayBlue. But they are proof, right now, that owning product and price beats curating other brands, at least so far in India. Their absence from PlayBlue's own competitive framing is a real gap, not because they compete unit-for-unit but because they are evidence against the Layer 3 thesis.

layers.title: Layer 3 · Sports Station (SSIPL) — the operating multi-brand comparator
layers.desc: ~₹172 Cr · 70+ stores, 50 cities · Nike, Puma, Adidas, Skechers, Asics, Reebok, plus own-label Mmojah

body.label: Position
body.text: The actual, operating Layer 3 peer — buys wholesale from multiple brands and resells under one roof, exactly PlayBlue's model, running today.

body.label: Why this matters
body.text: This is the demonstrated ceiling for pure multi-brand curation in India: roughly 4% of Decathlon's scale after years of operating. PlayBlue's competitive framing should name this comparator directly rather than treating the layer as unoccupied.

layers.title: Layer 3 · Planet Sports (Future Group) — the layer's largest prior attempt
layers.desc: 80 stores, 30 cities, ~₹50 Cr turnover at peak · wound down with Future Group's collapse

body.label: Position
body.text: India's largest-ever multi-brand sports chain by store count. Wound down for reasons tied to Future Group's broader collapse, not necessarily the model itself — a genuine ambiguity worth surfacing rather than resolving in either direction.

layers.title: Layer 3 · Foot Locker India — the newest entrant, and its format choice
layers.desc: Metro Brands (offline licence) + Nykaa Fashion (online), live since Oct 2024 · first South India store: 3,333 sq ft, Koramangala, Bengaluru

body.label: Position
body.text: The best-capitalised recent entrant into curated multi-brand sports/sneaker retail in India, backed by Metro Brands' ~50% gross / ~30% EBITDA margin discipline and exclusive-brand experience.

body.label: Why this matters
body.text: Given the capital and the licence to open at any scale, Metro Brands chose 3,333 sq ft for its first South India store — in the same city where PlayBlue is planning a 15,000 sq ft flagship. That divergence in format size deserves a direct answer, not an assumption.

layers.title: Layer 4 · Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Ajio — marketplaces
layers.desc: Aggregate many brands like PlayBlue does, but as a commission platform, not an inventory-owning curator

body.label: Position
body.text: Horizontal and fashion-led marketplaces carrying the widest sports assortment with the fastest national fulfilment. Online sports apparel demand on these platforms grew over 35% year on year in 2024. Ajio carries Decathlon. India's online fashion order volume rose more than 20.9% in FY24.

body.label: Relationship to PlayBlue
body.text: Structurally the nearest thing to "multi-brand" that exists at scale in India — but as a platform taking commission on third-party inventory, not a curator taking ownership and margin risk the way PlayBlue's stores would. They set the consumer's baseline expectation on price, selection and delivery speed, which is exactly what the 4-hour promise will be benchmarked against.

layers.title: Layer 5 · Unorganised and counterfeit retail — the real incumbent
layers.desc: Price-led, dominant outside metros, the actual base PlayBlue is converting from

body.label: Position
body.text: Unorganised and counterfeit retail continues to dominate large parts of the category. Buyers in tier-II and tier-III cities substantially prefer low-cost alternatives, and imitation jerseys, gym wear and athleisure are widely available at a fraction of branded prices.

body.label: Why it matters more than its place in the list suggests
body.text: PlayBlue is not primarily fighting Decathlon for share — it is trying to convert unorganised demand into organised demand at a materially higher price point. That is a slower, harder conversion than a share war between organised players, and it makes price perception the decisive variable.
